prize_parts.citation: For a visionary, densely patterned body of work, anchored in the Orbitor trilogy and Solenoid, in which memory, the body and dream are built into a vast metaphysical architecture.

statement.case_for: My preferred writer is unchanged: Mircea Cărtărescu, in a single-writer configuration. The citation is narrower than in round 1. On the common criteria, the case is distinctiveness of voice, formal and linguistic ambition, and imaginative depth sustained at very large scale. From public knowledge, the Orbitor trilogy (Blinding is its first volume) and Solenoid turn memory, the body and dream into one patterned metaphysical project. Attribution is clean: one author, one principal language, one coherent imaginative world. The chair asked which works should anchor the citation and whether it should name poetry. I now think it should be anchored in the large prose works and should not claim the poetry or early fiction as assessed evidence, because nobody in round 1, including me, claims to have assessed them. The wording 'body of work' leaves room for the wider oeuvre without asserting it. I give no weight to the six-of-six opening count as merit. The round-1 exchange did not move me to a different laureate. It did make me more careful about what the citation may claim.
statement.case_against: My main reservation is that the linguistic achievement, which is central to the case, is the part I can verify least. I know very long, dense Romanian prose through translation and public reception. I also cannot settle whether Solenoid and the later novels deepen the project or repeat it, and the evidence for the poetry and early work is thin. If that evidence showed the later work mainly elaborating the trilogy's method, the claim of sustained quality would narrow. Adonis's renewal of Arabic poetic language would then deserve a closer comparison. Carson's formal invention would deserve one too, if it holds on the written text alone. Neither comparison is closed, because my access to the Arabic is indirect and the Carson corpus is smaller and more fragmentary.

responses.point: Olsson wants the B007 citation to rest on the poetry and the novels together and to treat the poetry as a test of the oeuvre's unity. He ranks Adonis third and says the committee's own competence in Arabic is uncertain, so the Cărtărescu case is somewhat better supported by evidence we can actually weigh.
responses.response: I agree that the poetry is a real test of unity. Because it is a test, I would not write it into the citation until someone can report on it. That is why I have narrowed my wording to prose-anchored. If the committee can obtain a reliable account of the poetry, the citation can be widened. I also agree about the Arabic competence gap, and I share it. It is a reason for caution about Adonis, not a verdict on the work. Whether the regional expert reports mentioned in the chair's questions can close the gap is for the committee to establish, and I do not assume they can.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg says translation lowers confidence about Adonis's prosody and diction but not the documented scale of his reshaping of Arabic poetic language, so he would keep Adonis as a serious alternative and not rank him sixth, as I did.
responses.response: I accept part of this and have kept Adonis as my first alternative, as I did in round 1. I still ask what 'documented' means here. The scale of the renewal is documented through reception and commentary, which is real evidence of significance. The quality of the language is exactly what none of us can judge directly. I would not move him above Cărtărescu without a competent comparison of the later poetry with the foundational books. As you say, age and timing should not enter that comparison. My sixth place in the opening reflected how little I can assess, not a low view of the work.

responses.point: Sward's round-1 citation names prose only. She leaves open whether the later novels extend the originality of the earlier ones, and she warns that the citation would narrow considerably if the large novels do not sustain their quality across volumes.
responses.response: I move toward your wording. Your prose-only citation is more defensible than my 'prose and poetry', which claimed more than I have assessed. I have kept 'body of work' in place of 'prose' only so the citation does not exclude the rest of the oeuvre in advance. On your open question, I can report only that Solenoid is publicly described as intensifying the project, which is reception and not my reading. If the committee found the later volumes repetitive, I would narrow the citation further to the trilogy and Solenoid, and I would not fall back on the length of the career.

responses.point: Carlberg ranks Carson third and keeps her as an alternative. She says Carson's strongest claim rests on a smaller set of formally decisive books, and that Cărtărescu's sustained project is more securely a body of work. She wants any Carson citation tied to the written work.
responses.response: I agree, and this is the main reason Carson stays an alternative and not my first choice. The voice, the intellectual depth and the absence of a translation barrier are real advantages. The chair's question is whether the case stands on text alone once Nox as a book-object and the scholarly translations are set aside. I cannot answer that from what I know, and I do not think the committee has yet. If the remaining original corpus is shown to be large and sustained, I would reconsider. Until then I do not think her case can bear a whole-oeuvre citation as well as the Cărtărescu case can.

responses.point: Mattson resists letting doubt about late repetition turn into a preference for a more compact but narrower body of work. She treats scale combined with a singular voice as a strength and would welcome colleagues' book-level judgments.
responses.response: I agree that compactness is not a literary merit. Narrowing my citation to the trilogy and Solenoid is not a preference for a smaller project. It keeps the wording within what we have actually weighed. I would put the same test to every candidate, including the ones I rank lower. The test is whether recurrence is the method or a weakness, judged book by book and not by volume. I still hold my view that repetition belongs to the form in a project built on memory and the body, but it is a hypothesis and not a finding.

uncertainties: Whether Romanian syntax, rhythm and density carry in translation, so that my judgment of linguistic achievement may be overstated.
Whether Solenoid and the later novels extend or repeat the Orbitor trilogy. I cannot settle this without a full reading, and I rely on public reception.
How much of the poetry and early fiction exists in translation and has been assessed by anyone on the committee. I have therefore kept it out of the citation's explicit claims.
Whether the committee can obtain competent Arabic-language judgment of Adonis's later poetry against the foundational books, which my own access cannot supply.

Whether Carson's case stands on the written text alone, and whether Zurita's printed sequences carry his case without the landscape-scale works. I have not independently verified any source or read the full corpus of any candidate.
Carlberg's actual voting status is undocumented, so a six-member count depends on a modeling assumption. I do not treat the count as literary evidence.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. My work on Selma Lagerlöf and my own fiction are context, not evidence of favor for any shortlisted writer, and my ties to committee colleagues are ordinary professional ones. Nothing has changed since round 1. I have no listed tie to Cărtărescu, Adonis, Carson or any other shortlisted writer.
